notes: Completeness is strong: all five services exist, full CRUD is implemented for every entity, all three events (task.assigned, task.statusChanged, comment.added) are published, and the demo script exercises every endpoint with meaningful assertions. Code quality is solid — clean TypeScript interfaces, consistent immutable updates via spread, good error-message-driven HTTP status mapping, and readable structure throughout. However, several architectural and constraint violations drag the scores down. (1) Architectural Rule 1 (no direct service-to-service calls) is violated in the router: the router calls both `this.tasks.getById(taskId)` and `this.users.getById(authorId)` inside the POST /comments handler specifically to enrich notification data, then manually calls `this.notifications.createForUser(...)`. The router is acting as an orchestrator doing cross-service data resolution, which is the exact coupling the event bus is supposed to prevent. (2) The comment.added event subscription in NotificationService is effectively dead code for the assignee-notification use case — the real assignee notification is fired directly from the router, bypassing the event bus entirely for that notification. This means the event bus is not the sole inter-service communication channel. (3) The `comment.added` subscriber in NotificationService creates a self-notification for the author ('Your comment was posted by X') which is semantically odd and not in the spec. (4) Rule 3 (all HTTP handling in router only) is partially violated: `NotificationService.createForUser` is a public method that exists solely because the router needs to imperatively create notifications outside the event flow — it blurs the boundary of what belongs in the service vs. the router. (5) The router imports from TaskService and CommentService payload types, which is fine, but also imports TaskStatus directly — minor but indicative of tight coupling. (6) No email-uniqueness validation on user creation. These issues are not cosmetic; the comment notification flow is a genuine architectural compromise that the code itself acknowledges in inline comments, confirming the author was aware but chose expediency over compliance.
